clinician.trajectory_summary: A man in his 30s presented with a 3-week history of progressive patchy symmetric numbness and paresthesias in the legs and abdomen below the umbilicus, followed by lower extremity weakness and difficulty walking with two falls in the week before presentation. Clinical examination revealed absent vibratory sense and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, positive Romberg sign, wide-based gait, absent lower extremity reflexes, and patchy sensory loss to light touch and pinprick. Heavy nitrous oxide use (450 canisters daily for 4–5 months) and intermittently borderline B12 levels over 8 years were significant risk factors. Laboratory workup showed normal hemoglobin (140 g/L) with borderline macrocytosis (MCV 94 fL), normal serum B12 (672 pg/mL) but markedly elevated methylmalonic acid (5.86 µmol/L) and homocysteine (32 µmol/L), confirming functional B12 deficiency. Intrinsic factor blocking antibodies were present, establishing autoimmune atrophic gastritis as the underlying cause of B12 deficiency. MRI of the spine revealed patchy hyperintense T2 signal abnormality in the dorsal columns from C3 to T9-T10 without enhancement, consistent with subacute combined degeneration. Gastric biopsy confirmed chronic inflammation and reactive changes in the antral and oxyntic mucosa, consistent with atrophic gastritis, and was negative for giardia, coeliac disease, and Helicobacter pylori.
